Appendix A Optimal parameter pattern for weighed graphs

Here, we illustrate the pattern of optimal QAOA parameters for both weighted 3-regular (w3R) graphs and weighted complete graphs. The weight of each edge is randomly drawn from uniform distribution on the interval [0,1][0,1]. In Fig. 9, we illustrate the pattern by simultaneously plotting the optimal parameters for 40 instances. In both cases, we see a pattern analogous to what was found for unweighted 3-regular (u3R) graphs in Fig. 2(b), where γi∗\gamma_{i}^{*} tend to increase smoothly and βi∗\beta_{i}^{*} tend to decrease smoothly with i=1,2,…,pi=1,2,\ldots,p. The optimal parameter of graphs from the same class also appears to cluster together in the same range.

We observe that the spread of 𝜸→∗\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{*} for w3R graphs in Fig. 9(a) is wider than that for u3R graphs in Fig. 2(b). This is because the random weights effectively increase the number of subgraph types. Moreover, the larger value for 𝜸→∗\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{*} for w3R compared to u3R graphs can be understood via the effective mean-field strength that each qubit experiences.

For complete graphs in Fig. 9(b), we observe that 𝜸→∗\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{*} for different weighted graphs have a narrower spread as well as smaller value compared to both u3R and w3R graphs. This is because there is only one type of subgraph that every edge sees. The non-zero spread is attributed to the fact that there are random weights on the edges. We also expect this spread to vanish as problem size NN increases, when for a typical instance, the distribution of weights on the N−1N-1 edges incident to each qubits converges. The smaller value of 𝜸→∗\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{*} can also be understood via the effective mean-field strength picture, as each qubit interacts with all N−1N-1 other qubits.

Appendix B Details of heuristic optimization strategies

In the main text, we have proposed two classes of heuristic strategies called INTERP and FOURIER for generating initial points in optimizing QAOA parameters. Both INTERP and FOURIER strategies work well for all the instances we have examined. We have chosen to use FOURIER for the results in the main text due to the slight edge in its performance in finding better optima when random perturbations are introduced. We now explain how these strategies work in details, and compare their performances.

B.1 Interpolation-based strategy

In the optimization strategy that we call INTERP, we use linear interpolation to produce a good initial point for optimizing QAOA as one iteratively increases the level pp. This is based on the observation that the shape of parameters (𝜸→(p+1)∗,𝜷→(p+1)∗)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{*}_{(p+1)},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{*}_{(p+1)}) closely resembles that of (𝜸→(p)∗,𝜷→(p)∗)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{*}_{(p)},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{*}_{(p)}).

The strategy works as follows: For a given instance, we iteratively optimize QAOA starting from p=1p=1, and increment pp after obtaining a local optimum (𝜸→(p)L,𝜷→(p)L)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}_{(p)}^{L},\vec{\bm{\beta}}_{(p)}^{L}). In order to optimize parameters for level p+1p+1, we take the optimized parameters from level pp and produce initial points (𝜸→(p+1)0,𝜷→(p+1)0)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{0}_{(p+1)},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{0}_{(p+1)}) according to:

[𝜸→(p+1)0]i\displaystyle\left[\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{0}_{(p+1)}\right]_{i} =i−1p​[𝜸→(p)L]i−1+p−i+1p​[𝜸→(p)L]i\displaystyle=\tfrac{i-1}{p}\left[\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{L}_{(p)}\right]_{i-1}+\tfrac{p-i+1}{p}\left[\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{L}_{(p)}\right]_{i} (15)

for i=1,2,…,p+1i=1,2,\ldots,p+1. Here, we denote [𝜸→]i≡γi[\vec{\bm{\gamma}}]_{i}\equiv\gamma_{i} as the ii-th element of the parameter vector 𝜸→\vec{\bm{\gamma}}, and [𝜸→(p)L]0≡[𝜸→(p)L]p+1≡0[\vec{\bm{\gamma}}_{(p)}^{L}]_{0}\equiv[\vec{\bm{\gamma}}_{(p)}^{L}]_{p+1}\equiv 0. The expression for 𝜷→(p+1)0\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{0}_{(p+1)} is the same as above after replacing γ→β\gamma\rightarrow\beta. Starting from (𝜸→(p+1)0,𝜷→(p+1)0)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{0}_{(p+1)},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{0}_{(p+1)}), we then optimize (e.g., using the BFGS routine) to obtain a local optimum (𝜸→(p+1)L,𝜷→(p+1)L)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}_{(p+1)}^{L},\vec{\bm{\beta}}_{(p+1)}^{L}) for the (p+1)(p+1)-level QAOA. Finally, we increment pp by one and repeat the same process until a target level is reached.

B.2 Details of FOURIER[q,Rq,R] strategy

We now provide the details of our second heuristic strategy for optimizing QAOA that we call FOURIER. As described in the Sec. III.2 main text, here we use a new representation of the pp-level QAOA parameters as (𝒖→,𝒗→)∈ℝ2​q(\vec{\bm{u}},\vec{\bm{v}})\in\mathds{R}^{2q} where

γi=∑k=1quk​sin⁡[(k−12)​(i−12)​πp],βi=∑k=1qvk​cos⁡[(k−12)​(i−12)​πp].\begin{split}\gamma_{i}&=\sum_{k=1}^{q}u_{k}\sin\left[\left(k-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(i-\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{\pi}{p}\right],\\ \beta_{i}&=\sum_{k=1}^{q}v_{k}\cos\left[\left(k-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(i-\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{\pi}{p}\right].\ \end{split} (16)

Roughly speaking, the FOURIER strategy works by starting with level p=1p=1, optimize, and then reuse the optimum at level pp in (𝒖→,𝒗→)(\vec{\bm{u}},\vec{\bm{v}})-representation to generate a good initial point for level p+1p+1.

In fact, we propose several variants of the FOURIER strategy for optimizing pp-level QAOA: they are called FOURIER[q,Rq,R], characterized by two integer parameters qq and RR. The first integer qq labels the maximum frequency component we allow in the amplitude parameters (𝒖→,𝒗→)(\vec{\bm{u}},\vec{\bm{v}}). When we set q=pq=p, the full power of pp-level QAOA can be utilized, in which case we simply denote the strategy as FOURIER[∞,R\infty,R], since qq grows unbounded with pp. Nevertheless, the smoothness of the optimal parameters (𝜸→,𝜷→)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}}) implies that only the low-frequency components are important. Thus, we can also consider the case where qq is a fixed constant independent of pp, so the number of parameters is bounded even as the QAOA circuit depth increases. The second integer RR is the number of random perturbations we add to the parameters so that we can sometimes escape a local optimum towards a better one. For the results shown in the main text, we use the FOURIER[∞,10\infty,10] strategy, meaning we set q=pq=p and R=10R=10, unless otherwise stated.

In the basic FOURIER[∞,0\infty,0] variant of this strategy, we generate a good initial point for level p+1p+1 by adding a higher frequency component, initialized at zero amplitude, to the optimum at level pp. More concretely, we take parameters from a local optimum (𝒖→(p)L,𝒗→(p)L)∈ℝ2​p(\vec{\bm{u}}^{L}_{(p)},\vec{\bm{v}}^{L}_{(p)})\in\mathds{R}^{2p} at level pp, and generate a initial point (𝒖→(p+1)0,𝒗→(p+1)0)∈ℝ2​(p+1)(\vec{\bm{u}}^{0}_{(p+1)},\vec{\bm{v}}^{0}_{(p+1)})\in\mathds{R}^{2(p+1)} according to

𝒖→(p+1)0=(𝒖→(p)L,0),𝒗→(p+1)0=(𝒗→(p)L,0).\displaystyle\vec{\bm{u}}^{0}_{(p+1)}=(\vec{\bm{u}}^{L}_{(p)},0),\quad\vec{\bm{v}}^{0}_{(p+1)}=(\vec{\bm{v}}^{L}_{(p)},0). (17)

Using (𝒖→(p+1)0,𝒗→(p+1)0)(\vec{\bm{u}}^{0}_{(p+1)},\vec{\bm{v}}^{0}_{(p+1)}) as a initial point, we perform BFGS optimization routine to obtain a local optimum (𝒖→(p+1)L,𝒗→(p+1)L)(\vec{\bm{u}}^{L}_{(p+1)},\vec{\bm{v}}^{L}_{(p+1)}) for the level p+1p+1.

We also consider an improved variant of the strategy, FOURIER[∞,R>0\infty,R>0], which is sketched alongside the R=0R=0 variant in Fig. 10. This is motivated by our observation that the basic FOURIER[∞,0\infty,0] strategy can sometimes get stuck at a sub-optimal local optimum, whereas perturbing its initial point can improve the performance of QAOA. Here, in addition to optimizing according to the basic strategy, we optimize (p+1)(p+1)-level QAOA from R+1R+1 extra initial points, RR of which are generated by adding random perturbations to the best of all local optima (𝒖→(p)B,𝒗→(p)B)(\vec{\bm{u}}^{B}_{(p)},\vec{\bm{v}}^{B}_{(p)}) found at level pp. Specifically, for each instance at (p+1)(p+1)-level QAOA, and for r=0,1,…,Rr=0,1,\ldots,R, we optimize starting from

𝒖→(p+1)0,r={(𝒖→(p)B,0),r=0(𝒖→(p)B+α​𝒖→(p)P,r,0),1≤r≤R𝒗→(p+1)0,r={(𝒗→(p)B,0),r=0(𝒗→(p)B+α​𝒗→(p)P,r,0),1≤r≤R\displaystyle\begin{split}\vec{\bm{u}}^{0,r}_{(p+1)}&=\begin{cases}(\vec{\bm{u}}^{B}_{(p)},0),&r=0\\ (\vec{\bm{u}}^{B}_{(p)}+\alpha\vec{\bm{u}}^{P,r}_{(p)},0),&1\leq r\leq R\end{cases}\\ \vec{\bm{v}}^{0,r}_{(p+1)}&=\begin{cases}(\vec{\bm{v}}^{B}_{(p)},0),&r=0\\ (\vec{\bm{v}}^{B}_{(p)}+\alpha\vec{\bm{v}}^{P,r}_{(p)},0),&1\leq r\leq R\end{cases}\end{split} (18)

where 𝒖→(p)P,r\vec{\bm{u}}^{P,r}_{(p)} and 𝒗→(p)P,r\vec{\bm{v}}^{P,r}_{(p)} contain random numbers drawn from normal distributions with mean 0 and variance given by 𝒖→(p)B\vec{\bm{u}}^{B}_{(p)} and 𝒗→(p)B\vec{\bm{v}}^{B}_{(p)}:

[𝒖→(p)P,r]k∼Normal​(0,[𝒖→(p)B]k2),[𝒗→(p)P,r]k∼Normal​(0,[𝒗→(p)B]k2).\displaystyle\begin{split}\left[\vec{\bm{u}}^{P,r}_{(p)}\right]_{k}\sim\text{Normal}\left(0,\left[\vec{\bm{u}}^{B}_{(p)}\right]_{k}^{2}\right),\\ \left[\vec{\bm{v}}^{P,r}_{(p)}\right]_{k}\sim\text{Normal}\left(0,\left[\vec{\bm{v}}^{B}_{(p)}\right]_{k}^{2}\right).\end{split} (19)

There is a free parameter α\alpha corresponding to the strength of the perturbation. Based on our experience from trial and error, setting α=0.6\alpha=0.6 has consistently yielded good results. This choice of α\alpha is assumed for the results in this paper.

We remark that while the INTERP strategy can also get stuck in a local optimum, we find that adding perturbations to INTERP does not work as well as to FOURIER. We attribute this to the fact that the optimal parameters are smooth, and adding perturbations in the (𝒖→,𝒗→)(\vec{\bm{u}},\vec{\bm{v}})-space modify (𝜸→,𝜷→)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}}) in a correlated way, which could enable the optimization to escape local optima more easily. Hence, we consider here FOURIER with perturbations, but not INTERP.

Finally, we also consider variants of the FOURIER strategy where the number of frequency components qq is fixed. These variants are the same as aforementioned strategies where q=pq=p, except we truncated each of the 𝒖→\vec{\bm{u}} and 𝒗→\vec{\bm{v}} parameters to keep only the first qq components. For example, when optimizing QAOA at level p≥qp\geq q with the FOURIER[q,0q,0] strategy, we stop adding higher frequency components and use the initial point 𝒖→(p+1)0=𝒖→(p)L∈ℝq\vec{\bm{u}}^{0}_{(p+1)}=\vec{\bm{u}}^{L}_{(p)}\in\mathds{R}^{q}.

B.3 Comparison between heuristics

We now examine the difference in the performance among the various heuristic strategies we proposed. For our example instance in Fig. 11, we note that INTERP and FOURIER[∞,0\infty,0] strategies have essentially identical performance (except for small variations barely visible at large pp). This is expected since both strategies generate initial points for optimizing level p+1p+1 based on smooth deformation of the optimum at level pp. In any case, the FOURIER[∞,10\infty,10] strategy outperforms INTERP and FOURIER[∞,0\infty,0] beginning at level p≳20p\gtrsim 20. Interestingly, even when restricting the number of QAOA parameters to 2​q=102q=10, the FOURIER[5,10] strategy closely matches the performance of other heuristics at low pp and beats the R=0R=0 heuristic at large pp. This suggests that the optimal QAOA parameters may in fact live in a small-dimensional manifold. Therefore, optimization for intermediate pp-level QAOA can be dramatically simplified by using our new parameterization (𝒖→,𝒗→CLOSE(\vec{\bm{u}},\vec{\bm{v}}).

Appendix C Time-to-solution (TTS) for example graph instance

In Sec. V.2, we focused on a representative graph instance where the adiabatic minimum gap is small [Fig. 6(b)]. The low energy spectrum for the graph along the QA path can be seen in Fig. 12(a). We remark that only eigenstates that are invariant under the parity operator 𝒫=∏i=1Nσix\mathcal{P}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{i}^{x} are shown, since the Hamiltonian HQA​(s)H_{\text{QA}}(s) commutes with 𝒫\mathcal{P} and the initial state is 𝒫\mathcal{P}-invariant: 𝒫​|ψ⁡(0)⟩=|ψ⁡(0)⟩\mathcal{P}|\psi(0)\rangle=|\psi(0)\rangle.

Fig. 12(b) and Fig. 12(c) illustrate TTSQA\text{TTS}_{\text{QA}} and TTSQAOA\text{TTS}_{\text{QAOA}} for the same graph. For QA, one can see that non-adiabatic evolution with T≈20T\approx 20 yields orders of magnitude shorter TTS than the adiabatic evolution. We also see that TTS in the adiabatic limit is independent of the annealing time TT, following the Landau-Zener formula pGS=1−exp⁡(−c​T​Δmin2)p_{\text{GS}}=1-\exp\left(-cT\Delta_{\min}^{2}\right). For QAOA, we use our FOURIER[∞,10\infty,10] heuristic strategy to perform the numerical simulation up to pmax=50p_{\max}=50, and compute TTSQAOA​(p)\text{TTS}_{\text{QAOA}}(p) and TTSQAOAopt\text{TTS}_{\text{QAOA}}^{\text{opt}} (up to p≤pmaxp\leq p_{\max}). For this particular graph, we note that although TTSQAOAopt\text{TTS}_{\text{QAOA}}^{\text{opt}} occurs at p=49p=49, in practice it may be better to run QAOA at p=4p=4 or p=5p=5 due to optimization overhead and error accumulation at deeper circuit depths. The apparent discontinuous jump in TTSQAOA\text{TTS}_{\text{QAOA}} is due to the corresponding jump in pGS​(p)p_{\text{GS}}(p), which can be explained by two reasons: first, our heuristic strategy is not guaranteed to find the global optimum, and random perturbations may help the algorithm escape a local optimum, resulting in a jump in ground state population; second, even when the global optimum is found for all level pp, there can still be discontinuities in pGSp_{\text{GS}}, since the objective function of QAOA is energy instead of ground state population.

Appendix D Effective few-level understanding of the diabatic bump

In this Appendix, we elucidate the mechanism of the diabatic bump observed in Fig. 6(c) via an effective few-level dynamics. To study the intermediate dynamics during quantum annealing, we can work in the basis of instantaneous eigenstates |ϵl​(t)⟩|\epsilon_{l}(t)\rangle, where

HQA​(t)​|ϵl​(t)⟩=ϵl​(t)​|ϵl​(t)⟩.H_{\text{QA}}(t)|\epsilon_{l}(t)\rangle=\epsilon_{l}(t)|\epsilon_{l}(t)\rangle. (20)

Expanding the time-evolved state in this basis as |ψ⁡(t)⟩=∑lal​(t)​|ϵl​(t)⟩|\psi(t)\rangle=\sum_{l}a_{l}(t)|\epsilon_{l}(t)\rangle, the Schrodinger equation can be written as

i​∑l(a˙l​|ϵl⟩+al​|ϵ˙l⟩)=∑lϵl​al​|ϵl⟩,i\sum_{l}\left(\dot{a}_{l}|\epsilon_{l}\rangle+a_{l}|\dot{\epsilon}_{l}\rangle\right)=\sum_{l}\epsilon_{l}a_{l}|\epsilon_{l}\rangle, (21)

where ℏ=1\hbar=1 and the time dependence in the notations is dropped for convenience. Multiplying the equation by ⟨ϵk|\langle\epsilon_{k}|, the Schrodinger equation becomes

i​a˙k=ϵk​ak−i​∑l≠kal​⟨ϵk|ϵ˙l⟩,i\dot{a}_{k}=\epsilon_{k}a_{k}-i\sum_{l\neq k}a_{l}\langle\epsilon_{k}|\dot{\epsilon}_{l}\rangle, (22)

where ⟨ϵk|ϵ˙k⟩=0\langle\epsilon_{k}|\dot{\epsilon}_{k}\rangle=0 is taken by absorbing the phase into the eigenvector |ϵk⟩|\epsilon_{k}\rangle. Written in a matrix form, we have

i⁡(a˙0a˙1a˙2⋮)=(0−i⁡⟨ϵ0|ϵ˙1⟩−i⁡⟨ϵ0|ϵ˙2⟩⋯−i⁡⟨ϵ1|ϵ˙0⟩Δ10−i⁡⟨ϵ1|ϵ˙2⟩⋯−i⁡⟨ϵ2|ϵ˙0⟩−i⁡⟨ϵ2|ϵ˙1⟩Δ20⋯⋮⋮⋮⋱)​(a0a1a2⋮),\displaystyle i\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\dot{a}_{0}\\ \dot{a}_{1}\\ \dot{a}_{2}\\ \vdots\end{array}\right)\!=\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{cccc}0&-i\langle\epsilon_{0}|\dot{\epsilon}_{1}\rangle&-i\langle\epsilon_{0}|\dot{\epsilon}_{2}\rangle&\!\!\cdots\\ -i\langle\epsilon_{1}|\dot{\epsilon}_{0}\rangle&\Delta_{10}&-i\langle\epsilon_{1}|\dot{\epsilon}_{2}\rangle&\!\!\cdots\\ -i\langle\epsilon_{2}|\dot{\epsilon}_{0}\rangle&-i\langle\epsilon_{2}|\dot{\epsilon}_{1}\rangle&\Delta_{20}&\!\!\cdots\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\!\!\ddots\end{array}\!\right)\!\!\left(\begin{array}[]{c}a_{0}\\ a_{1}\\ a_{2}\\ \vdots\end{array}\right),

where we take the ground state energy ϵ0=0\epsilon_{0}=0 (by absorbing it into the phase of the coefficients) and Δi​0=ϵi−ϵ0\Delta_{i0}=\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{0} is the instantaneous energy gap from the iith excited state to the ground state. The time evolution starts from the initial ground state with a0=1a_{0}=1 and ai=0a_{i}=0 for i≠0i\neq 0, and the adiabatic condition to prevent coupling to excited states is

|⟨ϵ0|ϵ˙i⟩|Δi​0=|⟨ϵ0|d​HQAd​t|ϵi⟩|Δi​02=|⟨ϵ0|d​HQAd​s|ϵi⟩|Δi​02​T≪1.\dfrac{\left|\langle\epsilon_{0}|\dot{\epsilon}_{i}\rangle\right|}{\Delta_{i0}}=\dfrac{\left|\langle\epsilon_{0}|\frac{dH_{\text{QA}}}{dt}|\epsilon_{i}\rangle\right|}{\Delta_{i0}^{2}}=\dfrac{\left|\langle\epsilon_{0}|\frac{dH_{\text{QA}}}{ds}|\epsilon_{i}\rangle\right|}{\Delta_{i0}^{2}T}\ll 1. (35)

The first equality can be derived from Eq. (20). This produces the standard adiabatic condition T=O⁡(1/Δmin2)T=O(1/\Delta_{\min}^{2}). As we discussed in section V.2, the minimum gap for some graphs can be exceedingly small, so the adiabatic limit is not practical. However, it may be possible to choose an appropriate run time TT, which breaks adiabaticity, but is long enough such that only few excited states are effectively involved in the dynamics. This is the regime where the diabatic bump operates and one can understand the dynamics by truncating Eq. (D) to the first few basis states.

As an example, we plot in Fig. 13(a) the instantaneous eigenstate populations of the first few states. It is simulated with the full Hilbert space, but effectively the same dynamics will be generated if the simulation is restricted to the first few basis states in Eq. (D). Fig. 13(b) shows the strength of the couplings between the instantaneous ground state and the low excited states. By comparing Fig. 13(a) and Fig. 13(b), one can see that T=T∗=40T=T^{*}=40 allows the time evolution to break the adiabatic condition before the anticrossing: population leaks to the first excited state, which becomes the ground state after the anticrossing. Thus, the time scale of T∗T^{*} for the diabatic bump represents a delicate balance between allowing population to leak out of the ground state and suppressing excessive population leakage, which explains why it happens at a certain range of time scale.

Appendix E Comparing different classical optimization routines

In this appendix, we compare three different classical routines that can be used to optimize QAOA parameters: Bayesian Optimization [40], Nelder-Mead [39], and BFGS [33, *BFGS2, *BFGS3, *BFGS4]. This comparison is done by a numerical experiment where we apply these optimization routines to 10 instances of 14-vertex weighted 3-regular (w3R) graphs. To compare them on equal footing, we terminate each optimization run after a budget of 20​p20p objective function evaluations is used. In the gradient-based routine, BFGS, we include the cost of gradient estimation via the finite-difference method into the budget of 20​p20p objective function evaluations. For each routine, we start at p=1p=1 and gradually increment pp, and perform optimization where the initial point is generated using either our heuristic strategies (FOURIER and INTERP) or the standard strategy of random initialization (RI). We use the versions of these optimization routines implemented in MATLAB R2017b as bayesopt, fminsearch, and fminunc, respectively. The objective function at each set of parameter is evaluated to floating point precision. The tolerance in both objective function value and step size in parameter space, as well as the finite-difference-gradient step size, are chosen to be 0.01.

The result of our numerical experiment is plotted in Fig. 14. Similar to Fig. 3(a), we see that the average quality of local optimum found from 50 RI runs is much worse than the best, indicating the difficulty of optimizing in the QAOA parameter landscape without a good initial point. We also see, regardless of the classical routines chosen, one run of optimization from an initial point generated from our heuristic strategies is generally better than the best out of 50 runs from randomly generated initial points. This indicates that our heuristic strategies work much better than RI and can be integrated with a variety of classical optimization routines. Moreover, we find that Bayesian Optimization typically does not do as well as Nelder-Mead or BFGS for larger pp, which is consistent with the folklore that this routine is better suited for low-dimensional parameter space [40]. On the other hand, it seems both Nelder-Mead and BFGS have comparable performance, even when the cost of gradient evaluation is taken into account. The slight difference we observe between the two in Fig. 14 is inconclusive and can be attributed to sub-optimal choices of tolerance and step size parameters and the deliberately limited budget of objective function evaluations.

Appendix F Details of Simulation with Measurement Projection Noise

When running QAOA on actual quantum devices, the objective function is evaluated by averaging over many measurement outcomes, and consequently its precision is limited by the so-called measurement projection noise from quantum fluctuations. We account for this effect by performing full Monte-Carlo simulations of actual measurements, where the simulated quantum processor only outputs approximate values of the objective function obtained by averaging MM measurements:

F¯p,M=1M​∑i=1MC⁡(𝒛p,i),\bar{F}_{p,M}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}C(\bm{z}_{p,i}), (36)

where 𝒛p,i\bm{z}_{p,i} is a random variable corresponding to the iith measurement outcome obtained by measuring |ψp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)⟩|\psi_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})\rangle in the computational basis, and C⁡(𝒛)C(\bm{z}) is the classical objective function. Note when M→∞M\to\infty, we obtain F¯p,M→Fp=⟨ψp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)|HC|ψp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)⟩\bar{F}_{p,M}\to F_{p}=\langle\psi_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})|H_{C}|\psi_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})\rangle. In the simulation, we achieve finite precision |F¯p,M−Fp|≲ξ|\bar{F}_{p,M}-F_{p}|\lesssim\xi by sampling measurements until the cumulative standard error of the mean falls below the target precision level ξ\xi. In other words, for each evaluation of FpF_{p} requested by the classical optimizer, the number of measurements MM performed is set by the following criterion:

1M⁡(M−1)​∑i=1M[C⁡(𝒛p,i)−F¯p,M]2≤ξ.\sqrt{\frac{1}{M(M-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{M}[C(\bm{z}_{p,i})-\bar{F}_{p,M}]^{2}}\leq\xi. (37)

Roughly, we expect M≈Var⁡(Fp)/ξ2M\approx\Var(F_{p})/\xi^{2}. To address issues with finite sample sizes, we also require that at least 10 measurements be performed (M≥10M\geq 10) for each objective function evaluation.

We now provide some details on the classical optimization algorithm used to optimize QAOA parameters. Generally, classical optimization algorithms iteratively uses information from some given parameter point (𝜸→,𝜷→)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}}) to find a new parameter point (𝜸→′,𝜷→′)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{\prime},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{\prime}) that hopefully produces a larger value of the objective function Fp​(𝜸→′,𝜷→′)≥Fp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)F_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{\prime},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{\prime})\geq F_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}}). In order for the algorithm to terminate, we need to set some stopping criteria. Here, we specify two: First, we set an objective function tolerance ϵ\epsilon, such that if the change in objective function |F¯p,M′​(𝜸→′,𝜷→′)−F¯p,M​(𝜸→,𝜷→)|≤ϵ|\bar{F}_{p,M^{\prime}}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{\prime},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{\prime})-\bar{F}_{p,M}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})|\leq\epsilon, the algorithm terminates. We also set a step-tolerance δ\delta, so that the algorithm terminates if the new parameter point is very close to the previous one |𝜸→′−𝜸→|2+|𝜷→′−𝜷→|2≤δ2|\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{\prime}-\vec{\bm{\gamma}}|^{2}+|\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{\prime}-\vec{\bm{\beta}}|^{2}\leq\delta^{2}. For gradient-based optimization algorithms such as BFGS, we also use δ\delta as the increment size for estimating gradients via the finite-difference method: ∂Fp/∂γi≃[F¯p,M′​(γi+δ)−F¯p,M​(γi)]/δ\partial F_{p}/\partial\gamma_{i}\simeq[\bar{F}_{p,M^{\prime}}(\gamma_{i}+\delta)-\bar{F}_{p,M}(\gamma_{i})]/\delta. In our simulations, we use the BFGS algorithm implemented as fminunc in the standard library of MATLAB R2017b.

Using the approach described above, we simulate experiments of optimizing QAOA with measurement projection noise for a few example instances, with various choices of precision parameters (ϵ,ξ,δ)(\epsilon,\xi,\delta) and initial points. For the representative instance studied in Fig. 7, we set ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1, ξ=0.05\xi=0.05, and δ=0.01\delta=0.01. In each run of the simulated experiment, we start with QAOA of level either p=1p=1 or p=5p=5, and optimize increasing levels of QAOA using our FOURIER[∞,0\infty,0] heuristic strategy. The initial point of QAOA optimization is either randomly selected (when starting at p=1p=1) or chosen based on an educated guess using optimal parameters from small-sized instances (at p=1p=1 and p=5p=5). Specifically, the educated guess for the initial points we use are (𝒖→0,𝒗→0)=(1.4849,0.5409)(\vec{\bm{u}}^{0},\vec{\bm{v}}^{0})=(1.4849,0.5409) at level p=1p=1, and

𝒖→0\displaystyle\vec{\bm{u}}^{0} =(1.9212,0.2891,0.1601,0.0564,0.0292),\displaystyle=(1.9212,0.2891,0.1601,0.0564,0.0292), (38)
𝒗→0\displaystyle\vec{\bm{v}}^{0} =(0.6055,−0.0178,0.0431,−0.0061,0.0141)\displaystyle=(0.6055,-0.0178,0.0431,-0.0061,0.0141) (39)

at level p=5p=5. For each such run, we keep track of the history of all the measurements, so that the largest cut Cuti\text{Cut}_{i} found after the ii-th measurement can be calculated. We repeat each experiment for 500 times with different pseudo-random number generation seeds, and average over their histories.

Appendix G Techniques to speed up numerical simulation

In this Appendix, we discuss a number of techniques we exploited to speed up the numerical simulation for both QAOA and QA.

First, we make use of the symmetries present in the Hamiltonian. For general graphs, the only symmetry operator that commutes with both HCH_{C} and HBH_{B} is the parity operator 𝒫=∏i=1Nσix\mathcal{P}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{i}^{x}: [HC,𝒫]=0,[HB,𝒫]=0[H_{C},\mathcal{P}]=0,[H_{B},\mathcal{P}]=0, and so does [HQA​(s),𝒫]=0[H_{\text{QA}}(s),\mathcal{P}]=0, where HQA​(s)H_{\text{QA}}(s) is the quantum annealing Hamiltonian in Eq. (9). The parity operator has two eigenvalues, +1+1 and −1-1, each with half of the entire Hilbert space. The initial state for both QAOA and QA is in the positive sector, i.e., 𝒫​|+⟩⊗N=|+⟩⊗N\mathcal{P}|+\rangle^{\otimes N}=|+\rangle^{\otimes N}. Thus, any dynamics remain in the positive parity sector. We can rewrite HCH_{C} and HBH_{B} in the basis of the eigenvectors of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and reduce the Hilbert space from 2N2^{N} to 2N−12^{N-1} by working in the positive parity sector.

For QA, dynamics involving the time-dependent Hamiltonian can be simulated by dividing the total simulation time TT into sufficiently small discrete time τ\tau and implement each time step sequentially. At each small step, one can evolve the state without forming the full evolution operator [75], either using Krylov subspace projection method [76] or a truncated Taylor series approximation [77]. In our simulation, we used a scaling and squaring method with a truncated Taylor series approximation [77] as it appears to run slightly faster than the Krylov subspace method for small time steps.

For QAOA, the dynamics can be implemented in a more efficient way due to the special form of the operators HCH_{C} and HBH_{B}. We work in the standard σz\sigma_{z} basis. Thus, HC=∑⟨i,j⟩wi​j2​(𝟙−σiz​σjz)H_{C}=\sum_{\left<i,j\right>}\frac{w_{ij}}{2}(\mathds{1}-\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}) can be written as a diagonal matrix and the action of e−i​γ​HCe^{-i\gamma H_{C}} can be implemented as vector operations. For HBH_{B}, the time evolution operator can be simplified as

e−i​β​HB=∏j=1Ne−i​β​σjx=∏j=1N(𝟙​cos⁡β−i​σjx​sin⁡β).e^{-i\beta H_{B}}=\prod_{j=1}^{N}e^{-i\beta\sigma_{j}^{x}}=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\left(\mathds{1}\cos\beta-i\sigma_{j}^{x}\sin\beta\right). (40)

Therefore, the action of e−i​β​HBe^{-i\beta H_{B}} can also be implemented as NN sequential vector operations without explicitly forming the sparse matrix HBH_{B}, which both improves simulation speed and saves memory. In addition, in the optimization of variational parameters, we calculated the gradient analytically, instead of using finite-difference methods. Techniques similar to the gradient ascent pulse engineering (GRAPE) method [78] were used, which reduces the cost of computing the gradient from O⁡(p2)O(p^{2}) to O⁡(p)O(p), for a pp-level QAOA. Lastly, in our FOURIER strategy, we need to calculate the gradient of the objective function with respect to the new parameters (𝒖→,𝒗→)(\vec{\bm{u}},\vec{\bm{v}}). Since 𝜸→=AS​𝒖→\vec{\bm{\gamma}}=A_{S}\vec{\bm{u}} and 𝜷→=AC​𝒗→\vec{\bm{\beta}}=A_{C}\vec{\bm{v}} for some matrices ASA_{S} and ACA_{C}, their gradients are also related via ∇𝒖→=AS​∇𝜸→\nabla_{\vec{\bm{u}}}=A_{S}\nabla_{\vec{\bm{\gamma}}} and ∇𝒗→=AS​∇𝜷→\nabla_{\vec{\bm{v}}}=A_{S}\nabla_{\vec{\bm{\beta}}}.

Appendix H QAOA for Maximum Independent Set

In this Appendix, we briefly illustrate the generality of our results by applying QAOA to another class of combinatorial optimization problems called Maximum Independent Set (MIS). Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), the MIS problem concerns finding the largest independent set—a subset of vertices where no two of which share an edge. In other words, the problem Hamiltonian is

HP=𝒫IS​(∑in^i)​𝒫ISH_{P}=\mathcal{P}_{\rm IS}\left(\sum_{i}\hat{n}_{i}\right)\mathcal{P}_{\rm IS} (41)

where n^=|1⟩​⟨1|=(𝟙−σz)/2\hat{n}=|1\rangle\langle 1|=(\mathds{1}-\sigma^{z})/2, and 𝒫IS\mathcal{P}_{\rm IS} is the projection (or restriction) onto the subspace of independent set states span​{|ψ⟩:n^i​n^j​|ψ⟩=0​∀(i,j)∈E}\text{span}\{|\psi\rangle:\hat{n}_{i}\hat{n}_{j}|\psi\rangle=0~\forall(i,j)\in E\}. The pp-level QAOA for MIS, first suggested by [2], involves the preparation of the following variational wavefunction

|ψp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)⟩=e−i​βp​HQ​∏k=1p−1e−i​γk​HP​e−i​βk​HQ​|0⟩⊗N,\vskip-5.0pt|\psi_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})\rangle=e^{-i\beta_{p}H_{Q}}\prod_{k=1}^{p-1}e^{-i\gamma_{k}H_{P}}e^{-i\beta_{k}H_{Q}}|0\rangle^{\otimes N}, (42)

where

HQ=𝒫IS​(∑iσix)​𝒫IS.H_{Q}=\mathcal{P}_{\rm IS}\left(\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{x}\right)\mathcal{P}_{\rm IS}. (43)

Similar to the case of MaxCut, here QAOA works by repeatedly measuring the system in the computational basis to obtain an estimate of Gp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)=⟨ψp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)|HP|ψp​(𝜸→,𝜷→)⟩G_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})=\langle\psi_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})|H_{P}|\psi_{p}(\vec{\bm{\gamma}},\vec{\bm{\beta}})\rangle, and using a classical computer to search for the best variational parameters (𝜸→∗,𝜷→∗)(\vec{\bm{\gamma}}^{*},\vec{\bm{\beta}}^{*}) so as to maximize GpG_{p}. We note the evolution can be implemented using the following physical Hamiltonian

HphysicalMIS​(t)=∑i[Δ⁡(t)​n^i+Ω⁡(t)​σix]+∑⟨i,j⟩U​n^i​n^j.H^{\rm MIS}_{\rm physical}(t)=\sum_{i}[\Delta(t)\hat{n}_{i}+\Omega(t)\sigma_{i}^{x}]+\sum_{\left<i,j\right>}U\hat{n}_{i}\hat{n}_{j}. (44)

In the U≫|Δ|,|Ω|U\gg|\Delta|,|\Omega| limit, the system is constraint to the manifold where n^i​n^j=0\hat{n}_{i}\hat{n}_{j}=0 for all edges ⟨i,j⟩\left<i,j\right> (since the initial state is |0⟩⊗N|0\rangle^{\otimes N}), and the QAOA circuit can be performed by setting appropriate waveforms of Δ⁡(t)\Delta(t) and Ω⁡(t)\Omega(t). See Ref. [49] for an implementation scheme of MIS with a platform of neutral atoms interacting via Rydberg excitations.

After performing exhaustive search of QAOA parameters using randomly initialized optimization for many instances of MIS, we discover a similar pattern. This is illustrated in Fig. 15(a), where we see that the optimal parameters at p=3p=3 tend to cluster in two visually distinct groups. For one of the groups, the smooth curve underlying the parameters exhibit resemblance to a quantum annealing protocol, using a time-dependent Hamiltonian:

HQAMIS​(t)=fP​(t)​HP+fQ​(t)​HQ.H_{\rm QA}^{\rm MIS}(t)=f_{P}(t)H_{P}+f_{Q}(t)H_{Q}. (45)

For example, if we choose (fP,fQ)(f_{P},f_{Q}) such that fP​(0)>0f_{P}(0)>0 and fP​(T)<0f_{P}(T)<0, and fQ​(0)=fQ​(T)=0f_{Q}(0)=f_{Q}(T)=0, then we can initialize the system in |0⟩⊗N|0\rangle^{\otimes N}, which is the ground state of HQAMIS​(t=0)H_{\rm QA}^{\rm MIS}(t=0), and evolve adiabatically to reach the ground state of HQAMIS​(t=T)∝−HPH_{\rm QA}^{\rm MIS}(t=T)\propto-H_{P} (i.e. state encoding the MIS solution). The Hamiltonian HQH_{Q}, which is turned on in the middle of the time evolution, induces couplings between different independent-set basis states and opens a spectral gap between the ground state and excited states. For concreteness of discussion, we focus on the following choice of annealing schedule:

fPc​(ξ)=6​(1−2​ξ),fQc​(ξ)=sin2⁡(π​ξ),ξ⁡(t)=t/T.f_{P}^{c}(\xi)=6(1-2\xi),~f_{Q}^{c}(\xi)=\sin^{2}(\pi\xi),~\xi(t)=t/T. (46)

We further analyze the performance and mechanism of QAOA for MIS by focusing on example instances that are difficult for adiabatic quantum annealing due to small spectral gaps. In Fig. 15(b), we show the level-crossing structure for such an example instance, where the minimum spectral gap is Δmin=0.0012\Delta_{\min}=0.0012. The same instance is studied in Ref. [49]. To study the performance of QAOA in deeper-depth circuits, we use the interpolation-based heuristic strategy outlined in Appendix B.1 to optimize QAOA parameters for this example instance starting at level p=3p=3. The performance of QAOA and quantum annealing are then compared in Fig. 15(c), where we see that QAOA is able to obtain a much larger ground state population in much shorter time compared to the adiabatic time scale of 1/Δmin2≈1061/\Delta_{\min}^{2}\approx 10^{6}. We then study the mechanism of QAOA by converting its parameters at level p=25p=25 to a smooth annealing path (fPQAOA,fQQAOA)(f_{P}^{\rm QAOA},f_{Q}^{\rm QAOA}) in a similar procedure as in Sec. V.2. This annealing path is visualized in Fig. 15(d), where we plot the effective ξeff​(t)\xi_{\text{eff}}(t) defined by fPc​(ξeff​(t))/fQc​(ξeff​(t))=fPQAOA​(t)/fQQAOA​(t)f_{P}^{c}(\xi_{\text{eff}}(t))/f_{Q}^{c}(\xi_{\text{eff}}(t))=f_{P}^{\rm QAOA}(t)/f_{Q}^{\rm QAOA}(t) for the QAOA-like schedule. We then monitor populations in the instantaneous eigenstates during the evolution to gain insights into the mechanism of QAOA. As shown in Fig. 15(e), QAOA is able to learn to navigate a very complicated level-crossing structure by a combination of adiabatic and non-adiabatic operations: the system diabatically couples to the excited states, lingers to maximize population in the fifth excited state, and then exploits a series of anti-crossings to return to the ground state. Our results here demonstrate that the non-adiabatic mechanisms observed in QAOA for MaxCut can play a significant role in more general problems, such as difficult MIS instances.
